stories.title: NASA's Swift Observatory re-enters after nearly 22 years of transient astronomy
paragraphs: ScienceDaily reports NASA materials stating that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re-entered Earth's atmosphere after nearly 22 years. NASA APOD and The Conversation place the event at 7:39 a.m. EST on Nov. 4, 2026, over North Sumatra, Indonesia, matching U.S. Space Force timing cited by ScienceDaily.

According to The Conversation, Swift launched in 2004 to chase gamma-ray bursts with gamma-ray, X-ray, and UV/optical telescopes and could slew about 50 degrees in under 75 seconds. ScienceDaily notes the mission outlasted its original two-year plan by more than a factor of ten.

APOD and The Conversation say solar-maximum drag lowered the ~600 km orbit and that a July 3, 2026 boost attempt failed; most of the spacecraft was expected to burn up. Outlets credit Swift with burst catalogs, supernova alerts, neutrino follow-up, and a 2025 hydroxyl detection on 3I/ATLAS.

image.credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab, via ScienceDaily
image.alt: Artist concept of NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory above Earth

stories.title: Hera returns first close-up of Didymos after NASA's DART impact
paragraphs: ESA reports that Hera's Asteroid Framing Camera captured its first close-up of the Didymos binary system from about 60 kilometers away; the agency posted the image on Nov. 5, 2026, and Space.com featured it on Nov. 6.

ESA describes Didymos as about 780 meters across and Dimorphos as about 151 meters, mostly in shadow in this frame. Principal investigator Patrick Michel said the view shows the far side relative to DART's pre-impact imagery, with the equatorial ridge plus new boulders, craters, and groove- or ridge-like patterns.

According to ESA, DART's Sept. 26, 2022 impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit by about 33 minutes. Mission scientist Michael Kueppers said debris may have crossed the roughly 1-kilometer gap to Didymos. ESA plans a detailed imagery reveal on Nov. 25, 2026.

image.alt: ESA Hera close-up of asteroid Didymos with Dimorphos partly visible

stories.title: Heme signatures reported in 115-million-year-old Aratasaurus bone
paragraphs: ScienceDaily and Science News cover a Curtin-led PNAS study reporting mineralized cell-like structures and heme-related chemistry inside ~115-million-year-old Aratasaurus museunacionali limb bone from northeastern Brazil.

Curtin materials say elemental maps and molecular analyses support hemoglobin-derived heme inside vascular canals, with hausmannite linked to preservation. Science News also reports collagen-associated amino acids and quotes Kliti Grice calling the result a landmark molecular window into extinct physiology.

Science News records skepticism from Mary Schweitzer that localization and morphology fully meet prior fossil-blood criteria; Grice replies that anatomy, mineralogy, and chemistry converge. Institutional partners listed by ScienceDaily include JAMSTEC, Brazil's National Museum, URCA, and Johns Hopkins.

image.credit: Victor O. Leshyk, via Science News
image.alt: Illustration related to fossilized dinosaur blood-cell structures

stories.title: FLIP processing recovers 51 Eridani b in archival JWST coronagraph data
paragraphs: Northwestern University says a Nature paper published Nov. 4, 2026, introduces Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), a digital-twin model of JWST that subtracts starlight after accounting for tiny telescope imperfections. Live Science and Space.com report Nov. 6 coverage of the same result.

According to Northwestern, FLIP improved faint-planet sensitivity by about 2 to 15 times versus standard methods on archival JWST observations of HIP 65426, 51 Eridani, and TYC 5899. The team reports a detection of giant exoplanet 51 Eridani b at 4.3 micrometers in data where conventional processing had not recovered it; Space.com notes the world was first found from the ground in 2015 and has roughly 11 Jupiter masses.

Lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez and co-author Jason Wang stress that FLIP uses optimization tools common in machine learning but is not an AI planet finder, because it embeds known telescope physics. Northwestern and Space.com say the approach could help reanalyze existing coronagraph data and support future missions such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

image.alt: JWST image comparison showing 51 Eridani b after FLIP starlight subtraction
